mcq.q: Which stage usually uses the most compute?
options: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
Preference tuning (DPO)
Pretraining
Evaluation of the final model
mcq.why: Pretraining over trillions of tokens dominates total compute by orders of magnitude.
distractors: SFT uses orders of magnitude less compute than pretraining.
DPO runs on comparison pairs after SFT, a small fraction of the compute.
Evaluation is small next to training.

mcq.q: What does a base model (after pretraining only) usually do?
options: Refuses every request it receives, by default
Calls tools to look up answers it does not know
Continues text, not reliably following instructions
Answers every question helpfully, as a chat model does
mcq.why: Pretraining teaches continuation; SFT and preference tuning make an assistant.
distractors: A base model has learned no refusal behaviour.
Tool use is taught later and wired up by an application.
Helpful answering comes from instruction tuning.

mcq.q: What is continued pretraining?
options: Training only the output layer on labelled examples
Prompt engineering with longer domain examples
Training on preference pairs from domain experts
More next-token training on domain text, such as legal or code
mcq.why: It shifts knowledge and vocabulary use, with a risk of forgetting general skills.
distractors: That is a form of fine-tuning a head, not continued pretraining.
Prompting changes no weights.
That is preference optimisation.

mcq.q: What does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) train on?
options: Curated instruction–response conversations
Only unit tests and their pass or fail results
Pairs of better and worse answers to a prompt
Random web pages for next-token prediction
mcq.why: It teaches the conversation format and helpful behaviour from examples of ideal answers.
distractors: That is a verifiable reward, used in RL.
That is preference data.
That is pretraining.

mcq.q: Preference optimisation trains a model on…
options: Hand-written rules that score each answer
Image labels from a classification dataset
Response comparisons, or checkable rewards
Next-token prediction on web text alone
mcq.why: RLHF and DPO use preferences; RL with verifiable rewards uses checks such as tests.
distractors: Rules may verify, but training uses comparisons or rewards.
Unrelated to language-model preference tuning.
That is pretraining.

mcq.q: Asked “Write a haiku about Kubernetes”, a base model replies “Write a haiku about Docker. Write a haiku about…”. Why?
options: It refuses to write poems about technical topics
It is broken and needs to be retrained from scratch
It has no vocabulary for the word Kubernetes
Lists of prompts are common online, so continuing one is likely
mcq.why: A base model continues text; it was not trained to treat the text as an instruction.
distractors: It did not refuse; it continued the text.
A base model doing this is behaving as trained.
It wrote the prompt fine; it just did not answer it.

mcq.q: Which starting checkpoint fits each job?
options: Both from the base model, so no instruct behaviour is lost
Format fine-tunes from instruct; continued pretraining from base
Both from random weights, to avoid inherited behaviour
Both from the instruct model, since it already follows instructions
mcq.why: Format tuning builds on assistant behaviour; continued pretraining extends the base model's knowledge.
distractors: A narrow-format fine-tune from base must re-teach instruction following.
That would mean pretraining from scratch.
Continued pretraining on raw text fits the base model.

mcq.q: Facts that change weekly and depend on who is asking are needed by an assistant. What should you use?
options: Continued pretraining on the facts every week
Permission-aware retrieval, not fine-tuning
A larger base model with more general knowledge
Fine-tuning weekly on the newest facts
mcq.why: Weights cannot enforce permissions and go stale; retrieval stays current.
distractors: Weights cannot hold per-user permissions, and weekly training is costly.
Your facts were never in its training data.
Fine-tuning is slow to update and ignores who is asking.

mcq.q: What is the main risk of continued pretraining?
options: It costs nothing beyond the original pretraining
Forgetting general skills if the data mix is unbalanced
It always improves every task the model knew
It removes the tokenizer's general vocabulary
mcq.why: Mixing in general data helps keep earlier abilities.
distractors: It costs real compute and data work.
It can make other tasks worse.
The tokenizer stays the same.

mcq.q: Why is customising an existing model affordable for most organisations?
options: Fine-tuning needs no data at all, only prompts
Pretraining has become cheap enough for most teams
Models customise themselves while they are used
Later stages need orders of magnitude less compute
mcq.why: Pretraining uses most of the compute; adaptation reuses it (chapter 13).
distractors: Fine-tuning needs data; it just needs far less compute.
Pretraining remains very expensive.
Using a model does not change its weights.

mcq.q: A legal-tech team has 5 GB of unlabelled contracts, and an instruct model that mishandles their clause vocabulary. They also need answers in a fixed JSON format. Which plan matches the training stages?
options: DPO on the contracts, choosing each one over a random web page
Pretraining a new model from random weights on the 5 GB
SFT on the raw contracts, treating each one as an assistant reply
Continued pretraining from the base model, then SFT for the format
mcq.why: Unlabelled domain text suits continued pretraining from base; the format is a behaviour taught by SFT on examples.
distractors: Preference pairs teach which reply is better, not domain language.
Far too little data for pretraining, and it discards the existing model.
Raw contracts are not instruction–response pairs.

mcq.q: The topic says pretraining uses over 95% of total compute. If pretraining took 1,000,000 GPU-hours, at most roughly how many GPU-hours did all later stages use together?
options: About 5,000
About 950,000
About 50,000
mcq.why: If pretraining is at least 95%, the rest is at most 5% of the total: 1,000,000 ÷ 0.95 × 0.05 ≈ 52,600.
distractors: That is 0.5%, a factor of ten too small.
That adds 5% on top; it is the total, not the remainder.
That is 95% of pretraining's own figure, not the later stages.

mcq.q: Training compute for N parameters and D tokens is roughly…
options: 2ND
6ND
N²D
ND/6
mcq.why: About 2ND for the forward pass and 4ND for the backward pass.
distractors: 2ND is the forward pass alone; training adds about 4ND for the backward pass.
Compute grows linearly in parameters, not with their square.
The 6 multiplies; it does not divide.

mcq.q: Using C ≈ 6ND, how much compute does training an 8B model on 15T tokens take?
options: About 7.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs
About 7.2 × 10²⁶ FLOPs
About 7.2 × 10²³ FLOPs
About 1.2 × 10²³ FLOPs
distractors: Three orders of magnitude too low.
Three orders of magnitude too high.
That leaves out the factor of 6.

mcq.q: At the Chinchilla-optimal ratio of about 20 tokens per parameter, how many tokens would an 8B model train on?
options: About 160 billion
About 1.6 trillion
About 8 billion
About 15 trillion
mcq.why: 8B × 20 = 160B tokens.
distractors: Ten times too many.
That is one token per parameter.
That is far past Chinchilla-optimal, as modern models are trained.

mcq.q: Why are modern models trained on far more tokens per parameter than Chinchilla-optimal?
options: Tokens cost nothing to collect, so more is always free
The Chinchilla result was wrong about compute-optimal training
A smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve, and serving dominates
More tokens reduce the training cost of a given model
mcq.why: Chinchilla minimises loss for a training budget; total cost includes inference.
distractors: Good data is scarce and costly.
It holds for a fixed training budget; the goal changed.
More tokens raise training cost.

mcq.q: What is MFU (model FLOPs utilisation)?
options: The memory used on each GPU during training
The share of peak hardware FLOPs actually achieved
The model's accuracy on its validation set
The share of parameters active for each token
mcq.why: 35–50% is typical for well-tuned large runs.
distractors: MFU measures compute, not memory.
It measures hardware efficiency.
That describes MoE routing.

mcq.q: 7.2 × 10²³ FLOPs at about 4 × 10¹⁴ FLOP/s per GPU is how many GPU-hours?
options: About 50 million
About 500,000
About 5,000
About 1.8 billion
mcq.why: 7.2×10²³ ÷ 4×10¹⁴ = 1.8×10⁹ GPU-seconds ≈ 500,000 GPU-hours.
distractors: Two orders of magnitude too high.
Two orders of magnitude too low.
That is GPU-seconds, not hours.

mcq.q: At an illustrative $2.50 per GPU-hour, what do 500,000 GPU-hours cost?
options: About $1.25 million
About $12.5 million
mcq.why: 500,000 × $2.50 = $1.25M, for the final run alone.
distractors: That divides instead of multiplying.
A factor of ten too high.
A factor of ten too low.

mcq.q: What is “annealing” in a data mixture?
options: Shuffling the whole dataset again at each epoch
Training at a high temperature to explore more
Upweighting high-quality data near the end
Removing all code data near the end of training
mcq.why: Mixtures are tuned with small experiments; quality data late in training helps.
distractors: Shuffling changes order, not proportions.
Temperature is a sampling setting, not a data mix.
Annealing upweights quality data; it does not drop a type.

mcq.q: A team repeats a small corpus many times to reach a large token count. What should they expect?
options: Better generalisation from seeing each example often
The same results as a corpus of that many unique tokens
Lower compute cost for the same number of tokens
Less than new data would give, and more memorisation
mcq.why: Tokens seen again carry little new information.
distractors: Repetition mostly increases memorisation.
Repeated tokens add less than new ones.
Compute depends on tokens processed, repeated or not.

mcq.q: What do scaling laws describe?
options: Exact accuracy on every downstream task, ahead of time
The best prompt to use for each task at a given size
Loss falling as a power law in size, data and compute
How tokenizers should be trained on a growing corpus
mcq.why: They are empirical relationships used to plan runs.
distractors: They describe loss, not task accuracy.
Prompting is unrelated.
Tokenizer training is unrelated.

mcq.q: Why mask user and system tokens during SFT?
options: To save GPU memory during training
So the model learns answers, not prompts
To speed up tokenisation of each record
Because PyTorch requires it for chat data
mcq.why: Loss on assistant tokens teaches the desired behaviour; predicting the user's words is not the goal.
distractors: Masking does not reduce memory; every token still goes through the model.
Tokenisation is unchanged.
It is a choice about what the model learns.

mcq.q: What does a chat template do?
options: Compresses the conversation to fit the window
Turns messages into the exact tokens the model was trained on
Removes the system prompt from each request
Translates messages into the model's language
mcq.why: Each model family has its own format; libraries apply it with apply_chat_template.
distractors: Templates add role markers; they do not compress.
The system prompt is kept and marked.
Templates format; they do not translate.

mcq.q: You fine-tune or serve with the wrong chat template. What happens?
options: The model becomes faster
Quality degrades silently
Nothing changes
Training fails with an error
mcq.why: The model sees a format it was not trained on, without any error message.
distractors: Speed is unaffected.
Formatting matters.
It usually runs without error.

mcq.q: In Hugging Face and PyTorch, what does the label −100 mean during SFT?
options: A negative example the model should avoid
The end of the training sequence
A padding token ID added by the tokenizer
Position ignored by the loss
mcq.why: Masked positions, such as the user's words, do not contribute to the loss.
distractors: −100 is not a preference signal.
End tokens are real token IDs.
Padding positions are often set to −100, but −100 means “ignore”, not padding.

mcq.q: Which is a common source of instruction data that needs a licence check?
options: Random noise added for robustness
Empty conversations used as padding
Your own handwritten demonstrations
Synthetic data from a stronger model
mcq.why: Some model licences restrict using their outputs to train other models.
distractors: Noise is not instruction data.
Empty records teach nothing.
You own those.

mcq.q: Which training objective is used for code completion inside a file?
options: Fill-in-the-middle
Masked image modelling
Mean squared error
Contrastive loss only
mcq.why: The model learns to generate a missing middle given the text before and after it.
distractors: That is for images.
That is a regression loss.
That trains embeddings.

mcq.q: What does a distillation loss do?
options: Trains the model on reward scores
Deduplicates the training data
Removes layers from the model
Matches a teacher's distribution via KL
mcq.why: The student learns from the teacher's full distribution, not just the right token.
distractors: That is RL.
Deduplication is data work, not a loss.
That is pruning.

mcq.q: In SFT conversations with tool calls, which part is usually masked from the loss?
options: The assistant's final reply
The assistant's tool-call arguments
Nothing; every token is trained
The tool results
mcq.why: The model should learn to write calls and replies, not to predict what tools return.
distractors: The final reply is what the model must learn.
The model must learn to produce correct arguments.
Training on tool results teaches the model to imitate the system.

mcq.q: Which function renders messages into a model's chat format in Hugging Face transformers?
options: model.generate(messages, chat=True)
datasets.load_dataset(messages)
tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages)
tokenizer.decode(messages, roles=True)
mcq.why: It applies the template stored with the tokenizer.
distractors: generate produces text; it does not format the input.
It loads datasets; it does not render templates.
decode turns IDs into text.

mcq.q: What should you check before launching an SFT run?
options: That the GPU is on and has enough free memory for the run
Render one example; confirm only assistant tokens have labels
Nothing; training itself will reveal any problems quickly
That the loss starts at exactly zero on the first batch
mcq.why: A wrong template or mask trains silently on the wrong tokens.
distractors: Necessary, but it does not catch silent data bugs.
Wrong masks train without errors and only show up as bad behaviour.
A zero starting loss would itself signal a bug.

mcq.q: After an SFT run, the assistant starts its replies by repeating the user's question and sometimes writes the system prompt back. What is the most likely data bug?
options: The chat template marked roles correctly but the data was too small
The tokenizer split the user's words differently from training
The learning rate was too low for the model to learn answers
The loss covered user and system tokens, not only the assistant's
mcq.why: Without masking, the model learns to predict the prompts too, so it reproduces them.
distractors: A small dataset gives weak answers, not echoed prompts.
Tokenisation does not make a model copy the prompt.
A low rate weakens learning; it does not teach the model to echo prompts.

mcq.q: What is the common starting point for web-scale text collection?
options: Only code
Only books
Common Crawl
A company wiki

distractors: Code is one source among many.
Books are one source among many.
Internal wikis are far too small and private.

mcq.q: What did datasets such as FineWeb-Edu show?
options: Only code data matters for capability
More tokens always beat better tokens
Quality filtering helps at the same token count
Filtering never changes model quality

distractors: The result was about filtering web text for quality.
Better tokens beat more tokens at the same count.

mcq.q: How are exact and near-duplicate documents usually found?
options: Exact: hashes; near: MinHash with LSH
By embedding similarity only, for both kinds
Exact: MinHash; near: hashes of the full text
By reading every pair of documents by hand
mcq.why: Hashes catch identical text; MinHash and LSH scale near-duplicate detection to billions of documents.
distractors: Embeddings are costly at this scale and not how exact copies are found.
That swaps the two methods.
Impossible at corpus scale.

mcq.q: Document A has n-grams {a, b, c, d}; document B has {b, c, d, e}. What is their Jaccard similarity?
mcq.why: Intersection 3 (b, c, d) ÷ union 5 (a–e) = 0.6.
distractors: That is not the ratio here.
They are not identical.
That divides by 4, one set's size.

mcq.q: How does MinHash estimate Jaccard similarity?
options: The share of hash functions whose minima match
By comparing the lengths of the two documents
By counting every word the two documents share
By embedding both documents and comparing vectors
mcq.why: It avoids comparing full n-gram sets.
distractors: Length says little about overlap.
That is an exact count, which MinHash avoids.
MinHash uses hashes, not embeddings.

mcq.q: What do LSH bands achieve?
options: They translate documents into one language
Only documents sharing a band get compared
They remove stop words before hashing
They compress documents to save storage
mcq.why: Comparing billions of documents pairwise is impossible; bucketing makes it feasible.
distractors: Bands are parts of the signature.
Stop-word removal is preprocessing.
They group candidates; compression is not the goal.

mcq.q: What is contamination?
options: Toxic content left in the training data
Personal data left in training logs
Duplicate documents in the training set
Benchmark questions leaking into training
mcq.why: It is detected by searching for n-gram overlap with test sets (8.6).
distractors: That is a safety filtering issue.
That is a privacy issue.
That is duplication.

mcq.q: You find 40 of 500 internal benchmark questions verbatim in your fine-tuning data. What should you do?
options: Remove the overlap and recompute the score
Train longer so the model generalises past them
Delete the whole benchmark and start over
Report the score as it is, with a footnote
mcq.why: Those 40 measure memorisation, not ability.
distractors: The overlap still inflates the score.
Removing the overlap is enough.
A contaminated score misleads.

mcq.q: A team assumes publicly reachable web text may be used for any training. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; anything on the public web is free to train on
Only images on the web are restricted, not the text
Copyright, terms, robots preferences and privacy laws still apply
Public text is always openly licensed once it is posted
mcq.why: Licensing and consent are an active legal area; read a model's data documentation (16.6).
distractors: Rights and laws still apply.
Text is covered by copyright too.
Most web text has no open licence.

mcq.q: Why deduplicate training data?
options: Duplicates improve generalisation
It speeds up inference afterwards
Duplicates waste compute and aid memorisation
It is required by the tokenizer
mcq.why: Repeated text is learned verbatim and adds nothing new.
distractors: They encourage memorisation instead.
Training data does not affect inference speed.
Tokenizers do not need it.

mcq.q: Two documents have 128-hash MinHash signatures, and 96 of the minima match. What is their estimated Jaccard similarity?
options: About 0.75
About 0.25
About 1.33
About 0.96
mcq.why: The fraction of matching minima estimates Jaccard similarity: 96 ÷ 128 = 0.75.
distractors: That is the fraction that do not match.
That divides the wrong way; Jaccard similarity cannot exceed 1.
That reads the count of matches as a percentage.

mcq.q: What is preference data?
options: The model weights from each training run
Unlabelled web text used for pretraining
Two or more responses to a prompt, and which is better
A list of correct answers for each prompt
mcq.why: Judgements come from humans or from a model.
distractors: Weights are not data about preferences.
That has no judgements.
That is demonstration data for SFT.

mcq.q: What does a reward model output?
options: A probability for the next token
A score for a prompt–response pair
A chat template for the prompt
A new, better response to it
mcq.why: It is trained on preference data and used to score responses in RLHF.
distractors: The LLM outputs those.
Templates format inputs.
The policy generates responses.

mcq.q: In RLHF, why is a KL penalty to the original model used?
options: To make each training step run faster
So the policy does not exploit the reward model
To increase the length of the outputs
To remove the need for a reward model
mcq.why: Staying close to the reference limits reward hacking.
distractors: The KL term adds compute.
Length is not the target.
RLHF keeps its reward model.

mcq.q: What does DPO remove compared with RLHF?
options: The reward model and RL loop
The policy model being trained
The frozen reference model
The preference pairs themselves
mcq.why: A closed-form loss raises the preferred response's probability relative to a frozen reference.
distractors: DPO trains the policy directly.
DPO keeps the reference.
DPO trains on preference pairs.

mcq.q: When is RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) possible?
options: Only for image models with labelled data
Never for language models, only for games
Only when human raters score every output
When an automatic check can verify correctness
mcq.why: This is how reasoning models learn long chains of thought.
distractors: Code and maths are typical cases.
Reasoning models are trained this way.
Human scores are preferences, not verifiable rewards.

mcq.q: In GRPO, four sampled answers get rewards [1, 0, 0, 1]. With advantage = (reward − mean) / std, what are the advantages?
mcq.why: Mean 0.5 and standard deviation 0.5, so (1 − 0.5)/0.5 = 1 and (0 − 0.5)/0.5 = −1.
distractors: Those are the raw rewards.
That subtracts the mean but forgets to divide by the std.
That doubles the rewards.

mcq.q: What is reward hacking?
options: The model games the scorer, e.g. longer answers
Stealing the reward model's weights
Training the model without any rewards
A security attack on the training GPUs
mcq.why: Verifiers and reward models must be robust to it.
distractors: That is a security issue, not reward hacking.
That is not hacking.
Unrelated to rewards.

mcq.q: Your extraction reward gives full marks to any valid JSON. What will a model learn?
options: To output empty but valid JSON
To extract every field perfectly
Nothing
To refuse
mcq.why: Check field values, not just validity, so empty output scores zero.
distractors: The reward does not require correct fields.
